definition.text: Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive.

facts.text: The aim is a healthy, genetically varied, self-sustaining population where the species had died out, or a boost to an existing one.
Candidates are usually threatened or endangered, but reintroduction can also control pests, such as wolves curbing too many deer.
Individuals come either from wild populations (in situ) or from captivity such as zoos or botanic gardens (ex situ); wild sourcing is preferred where possible.
Source populations should resemble the release site genetically and ecologically so the animals or plants are well adapted.
Captive-bred animals can adapt to captivity, becoming tamer, less stress-tolerant and losing local adaptations.
Small reintroduced populations risk inbreeding, which can erode crucial genetic diversity.
There is no agreed definition of success, but it should produce viable, self-sustaining populations long term.
